# **Comprehensive Architectural Blueprint and Implementation Guide for the Internet HerokuApp Hybrid Automation Framework**

The discipline of software quality engineering has undergone a significant paradigm shift, transitioning from the era of rudimentary record-and-playback scripts to the development of sophisticated, enterprise-grade automation frameworks. The project, titled "The-Internet-Automation," stands as a definitive implementation of these modern engineering principles. It is specifically engineered to address the heterogeneous challenges presented by "The Internet" demo site on HerokuApp, a platform recognized globally as the benchmark for testing the limits of web automation tools. By successfully automating all forty-four scenarios—ranging from basic authentication and form handling to complex shadow DOM traversals and asynchronous resource loading—this framework serves as a rigorous demonstration of technical proficiency in a hybrid TestNG-Cucumber ecosystem.1

The foundational objective of this project is to provide a scalable, maintainable, and highly observable automation suite that adheres to the most stringent industry standards. At its core, the framework utilizes the latest Long-Term Support (LTS) release of the Java language, JDK 25, alongside Apache Maven 3.9.14 for build orchestration and IntelliJ IDEA 25.3.4 for development. This combination of tools ensures that the framework benefits from the most recent advancements in JVM performance, memory management, and IDE refactoring capabilities, positioning it as a future-proof solution for complex web testing requirements.3

## **Technical Foundations and the Java 25 LTS Ecosystem**

The strategic selection of Java 25 LTS as the primary programming language provides the framework with several architectural advantages. While previous versions like Java 21 established a baseline for modern language features such as virtual threads and record patterns, Java 25 focuses on refinement and efficiency, which are critical for high-concurrency test execution.4

### **The Impact of Java 25 on Automation Architecture**

The adoption of Java 25 allows the framework to leverage several key JEPs (JDK Enhancement Proposals) that directly influence the readability and maintainability of the automation code. For instance, the introduction of compact source files and instance main methods facilitates a reduction in boilerplate code when writing quick utility scripts or debugging driver configurations.5 Furthermore, the refinement of virtual threads—Project Loom—enables the framework to handle a high volume of parallel WebDriver instances with significantly reduced overhead compared to traditional OS-level threading models. This is particularly relevant when executing the forty-four scenarios of "The Internet" in parallel, as it ensures that the system resources are utilized optimally without sacrificing stability.4

| Technology Component | Version | Role in Framework |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Java JDK** | 25 LTS | Core Runtime and Performance Engine \[User Query\] |
| **Apache Maven** | 3.9.14 | Build Orchestration and Dependency Management \[User Query\] |
| **IntelliJ IDEA** | 25.3.4 | Primary IDE for Development and Refactoring \[User Query\] |
| **Selenium WebDriver** | Latest Stable | Browser Interaction and Protocol Handling 8 |
| **Cucumber-JVM** | 7.x | BDD Specification and Feature Orchestration 9 |
| **TestNG** | Latest Stable | Test Runner, Parallelization, and Assertions 10 |
| **ExtentReports** | 5.1.2 | Aesthetic Dashboard and Stakeholder Reporting 3 |

In addition to language features, the build management layer utilizes Maven 3.9.14 to centralize the lifecycle of the project. The pom.xml file is configured not just as a dependency list but as a control center for the entire framework, defining the compiler versions, surefire plugin configurations for TestNG suites, and the specific adapters required for ExtentReports and Cucumber integration.3 This level of structure ensures that any engineer cloning the project can achieve a "clean" build and execution environment within minutes, satisfying the critical industry requirement for project portability.12

## **Hybrid Framework Architecture: The Synergy of TestNG and Cucumber**

A hybrid framework model was selected to provide the best of both worlds: the descriptive, stakeholder-accessible power of Behavior-Driven Development (BDD) via Cucumber, and the robust execution and parallelization capabilities of TestNG.10 In professional environments, purely BDD frameworks often struggle with complex parallel execution logic, while purely TestNG-based frameworks may fail to provide clear visibility to non-technical stakeholders. This hybrid approach bridges that gap effectively.10

### **The Layered Design Pattern**

The architecture follows a strictly layered approach to separate concerns and enhance the reusability of code. This structure is essential for an interviewer to see that the candidate understands the difference between framework logic and test logic.16

1. **Feature Layer (Gherkin):** The forty-four scenarios are organized into ten logical groupings within .feature files. These files use Gherkin syntax—Given, When, Then—to describe the behavior of the application in plain English.1  
2. **Step Definition Layer:** This layer acts as the bridge, translating Gherkin steps into executable Java code. By using a "glue" package, the framework maintains a one-to-one mapping between the business language and the technical implementation.16  
3. **Page Object Model (POM) Layer:** Each page of the HerokuApp site is abstracted into a Java class. These classes contain the web element locators (using @FindBy annotations) and the methods that interact with those elements. This ensures that if a locator changes on the website, only a single class needs to be updated, rather than every test script.17  
4. **Utility and Support Layer:** This layer contains centralized logic for WebDriver management (DriverFactory), property file reading (ConfigReader), and common UI interactions (CommonActions). By using a ThreadLocal WebDriver instance, the framework ensures thread-safety during parallel execution, preventing conflicts between multiple browser windows.21

### **Orchestration with TestNG**

The framework utilizes TestNG as the primary runner, which allows for the configuration of execution parameters through a testNG.xml file. By extending the AbstractTestNGCucumberTests class in the TestRunner, the framework gains the ability to run Cucumber scenarios in parallel at the scenario level.21 This is a high-level architectural decision that drastically reduces the execution time of the entire suite, which is a major concern when scaling to forty-four or more scenarios in a CI/CD pipeline.10

## **Tactical Breakdown of the Forty-Four Automated Scenarios**

The comprehensive coverage of "The Internet" requires a framework capable of handling a diverse set of UI and network challenges. The scenarios have been grouped into ten distinct feature files, each focusing on a specific technological hurdle.1

### **Grouping 1: Advanced Authentication Mechanisms**

The framework handles more than just standard login forms; it addresses the complex protocols often found in enterprise security layers.

* **Basic and Digest Authentication:** These scenarios require passing credentials directly through the HTTP request. The framework handles this by constructing URLs in the format https://admin:admin@the-internet.herokuapp.com/basic\_auth, effectively bypassing the browser's native credential modal which Selenium traditionally struggles to interact with.1  
* **Form Authentication:** Utilizing Scenario Outlines and Examples tables, the framework validates both happy-path logins (e.g., tomsmith/SuperSecretPassword\!) and various failure modes, such as invalid usernames or passwords.1  
* **Forgot Password:** This scenario is unique as it expects a design-intended "Internal Server Error" (500), demonstrating the framework's ability to perform negative testing and assert on server-level failures.1

### **Grouping 2: Dynamic Web Behavior and Asynchronicity**

Modern web applications are rarely static. The scenarios in this group test the framework's ability to synchronize with the application state.

* **Dynamic Controls:** These scenarios involve elements that are added or removed from the DOM dynamically via AJAX. The framework utilizes explicit wait strategies—specifically WebDriverWait combined with ExpectedConditions—to ensure that the script does not attempt to interact with an element until it is in the desired state (e.g., visible, clickable, or gone).1  
* **Dynamic Loading:** The framework distinguishes between elements that are hidden in the DOM and those that are rendered only after a process completes. This tests the logic of "polling" mechanisms and fluent waits.1  
* **Disappearing Elements:** By using a retry logic within the page object, the framework handles the stochastic nature of elements that appear or disappear upon page refreshes, ensuring a robust test outcome regardless of the initial page load state.1

### **Grouping 3: Standard UI Components and Data Validation**

This grouping focuses on the reliability of standard HTML element interactions and the validation of data integrity.

* **Add/Remove Elements:** Validates the dynamic modification of the DOM by clicking an "Add" button multiple times and asserting the count of "Delete" buttons generated.1  
* **Sortable Data Tables:** This is a critical scenario for verifying data handling. The framework captures the contents of a table column, clicks the header to trigger a sort, and then verifies that the resulting list is in the correct alphabetical or numerical order.1  
* **Horizontal Sliders and Inputs:** Demonstrates the use of the Actions class and keyboard simulations (e.g., arrow keys) to precisely control slider values and numeric input fields.1

### **Grouping 4: Advanced User and Browser Interactions**

To prove senior-level proficiency, the framework automates interactions that go beyond simple clicks and typing.

* **Drag and Drop:** Using the Selenium Actions class to simulate mouse movements, the framework moves elements between columns (e.g., Column A to Column B) and verifies that the headers swap accordingly.1  
* **Context Menu:** Right-clicking on a specific "hot spot" to trigger a JavaScript alert, which is then accepted by the framework's alert handling utility.1  
* **Multiple Windows:** Handling the transfer of focus between the parent window and a newly opened child window, ensuring that assertions are made in the correct browser context before returning to the original page.1

### **Grouping 5 & 6: DOM Structures and Context Switching**

Complex DOM structures like iFrames and Shadow DOM represent significant hurdles for standard automation tools.

* **Nested Frames:** The framework navigates through a hierarchy of frames (Top \-\> Middle) to interact with text inside specific documents. This requires recursive context-switching logic that is central to the BasePage design.1  
* **Shadow DOM:** Since Shadow DOM elements are not accessible via standard XPath, the framework utilizes JavaScript executors to query the shadow root and locate elements, a key skill for modern front-end testing.1  
* **Challenging DOM:** Dealing with dynamic IDs that change on every reload, the framework relies on robust relative XPaths and CSS selectors that target stable attributes or text content.1

### **Grouping 7-10: File Management, Network Status, and Edge Cases**

The final groupings address the "non-UI" aspects of web testing.

* **File Upload/Download:** The framework verifies the ability to send local file paths to an upload element and asserts on the success message. For downloads, it ensures that files are retrieved and stored in a designated local directory.1  
* **HTTP Status Codes:** By navigating to specific status code endpoints (200, 301, 404, 500), the framework validates that the application correctly reports its state. This demonstrates an understanding of the relationship between the front-end display and back-end routing.1  
* **Broken Images:** Utilizing the HttpURLConnection or modern Java 25 HttpClient, the framework iterates through all images on a page to verify that their src attributes return a 200 OK status, identifying broken assets that would otherwise pass a visual check.1  
* **Geolocation and Mocking:** The framework demonstrates the ability to handle browser-level permissions and mock coordinates to verify location-based logic.1

## **Reporting and Observability: The Stakeholder Dashboard**

In a professional setting, the value of automation is often judged by the quality of its reporting. This project integrates two highly respected reporting libraries to provide total transparency into the test execution.29

### **ExtentReports (Spark Reporter)**

The primary dashboard is generated via ExtentReports 5.1.2. This reporter provides a rich, interactive HTML experience that includes:

* **Aesthetic Dashboards:** High-level pie charts showing the percentage of passed, failed, and skipped scenarios.9  
* **Detailed Logs:** Every Gherkin step (Given, When, Then) is logged with a timestamp and status.  
* **Automatic Screenshot Capture:** The framework is configured with an @After hook that detects a failed scenario, takes a screenshot, and embeds it directly into the report at the point of failure. This is invaluable for debugging flaky tests or environmental issues.9  
* **System Metadata:** The report automatically includes details about the environment, such as the Java version, OS, and browser configurations.27

![Extent Reports](screeshots/extentReport.PNG)

### **Cucumber-Reporting (Masterthought)**

For technical deep-dives, the cucumber-reporting (Masterthought) plugin is utilized. This tool generates statistics on the execution time of every feature, scenario, and step. It helps identify performance bottlenecks within the automation code and provides a clear audit trail for compliance and quality assurance reviews.29

![Cucumber Report](screenshots/cucumberReport.PNG)

## **Continuous Integration and the Jenkins Pipeline**

Running Jenkins via a .war file is a great way to keep things lightweight on Windows. Here are the concise, step-by-step instructions to get your project running.

### **1\. Launch Jenkins**

1. **Download:** Get the jenkins.war file from the [official Jenkins website](https://www.jenkins.io/download/).  
2. **Move file:** Place it in a dedicated folder, e.g., C:\\Jenkins.  
3. **Run:** Open Command Prompt in that folder and run:  
4. java \-jar jenkins.war  
5. **Unlock:** Look for the **initial admin password** printed in the console. Copy it.

### **2\. Browser Configuration**

1. **Open Port:** Go to http://localhost:8080 in your browser.  
2. **Setup:** Paste the admin password, select **"Install suggested plugins,"** and create your admin user.

### **3\. Configure Windows Tools**

Since you installed Java and Maven earlier, ensure Jenkins can see them:

1. Go to **Manage Jenkins** \> **Tools**.  
2. Find **JDK** and **Maven** sections.  
3. Click **Add JDK** / **Add Maven**, uncheck "Install automatically," and provide the paths you used in your Environment Variables (e.g., JAVA\_HOME).

### **4\. Create Your Project**

1. On the Dashboard, click **New Item**.  
2. Enter a name (e.g., "MyAutomationProject") and select **Freestyle project**. Click **OK**.  
3. **Source Code Management:** If your code is on GitHub, select **Git** and paste your Repository URL.

### **5\. Add Windows Batch Commands**

This is where you tell Jenkins exactly how to run your project.

1. Scroll down to the **Build Steps** section.  
2. Click **Add build step** \> **Execute Windows batch command**.  
3. In the text box, enter your commands. For a standard Java/Maven project, it usually looks like this:  
   mvn clean test   
4. If you need to run specific tags, looks like this:  
   mvn clean test \-Dcucumber.filter.tags="@auth"

## **6\. Run and Verify**

1. Click **Save**.  
2. Click **Build Now** on the left sidebar.  
3. Click the blue/red circle under **Build History** and select **Console Output** to see your batch commands executing in real-time.

### **Tip: Running Jenkins on a Different Port**

If port 8080 is busy, you can open a different port by starting the .war file like this:

java \-jar jenkins.war \--httpPort=9090

## **Operational Guide: Setting Up and Running the Framework**

To ensure that any evaluator can run the project without friction, the following instructions cover both graphical and command-line interfaces.

### **Environment Prerequisites**

Before beginning the setup, ensure the following are installed:

1. **JDK 25 LTS:** Download and set JAVA\_HOME.  
2. **Apache Maven 3.9.14:** Add to the system PATH.  
3. **Browsers:** Ensure Chrome, Firefox, or Edge is installed. The framework utilizes WebDriverManager (via Selenium 4 or a standalone library) to automatically manage driver executables.17

### **Execution from IntelliJ IDEA (GUI)**

IntelliJ IDEA is the recommended environment for development and debugging.

1. **Project Import:** Select "Open" and choose the project directory. IntelliJ will detect the pom.xml and prompt to import it as a Maven project.13  
2. **Maven Reload:** If dependencies do not download automatically, open the Maven tool window and click "Reload All Maven Projects".13  
3. **Running the Runner:** Locate src/test/java/runners/CucumberRunnerTest.java. Right-click the class and select "Run 'CucumberRunnerTest'." This will trigger the suite defined in the @CucumberOptions annotation.9  
4. **Running testNG.xml:** Right-click the testNG.xml file in the root directory and select "Run." This is the preferred method for executing with parallel threads.41

### **Execution from the Command Line (CMD/Terminal)**

Command-line execution is the industry standard for local batch runs and remote server triggers.To set up Java and Maven on Windows, you primarily need to install the files and then tell Windows where to find them using **Environment Variables**.

### **1\. Install Java (JDK)**

1. **Download:** Get the Windows x64 Installer from the [Oracle JDK site](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/) or [Adoptium](https://adoptium.net/).  
2. **Run Installer:** Follow the prompts (usually installs to C:\\Program Files\\Java\\jdk-xx).  
3. **Set JAVA\_HOME:** \* Search Windows for **"Edit the system environment variables"**.  
   * Click **Environment Variables**.  
   * Under **System variables**, click **New**.  
   * Variable name: JAVA\_HOME  
   * Variable value: C:\\Program Files\\Java\\jdk-xx (your actual path).

### **2\. Install Maven**

1. **Download:** Get the "Binary zip archive" from the [Apache Maven website](https://maven.apache.org/download.cgi).  
2. **Extract:** Unzip it to a permanent folder, e.g., C:\\maven.  
3. **Set MAVEN\_HOME:**  
   * In the same **Environment Variables** window, click **New** under System variables.  
   * Variable name: MAVEN\_HOME  
   * Variable value: C:\\maven\\apache-maven-x.x.x

### **3\. Update the Path Variable**

This allows you to run java and mvn commands from any terminal.

1. In **System variables**, find the variable named **Path** and click **Edit**.  
2. Click **New** and add: %JAVA\_HOME%\\bin  
3. Click **New** again and add: %MAVEN\_HOME%\\bin  
4. Click **OK** on all windows.

### **4\. Verify the Setup**

Open a **new** Command Prompt or PowerShell and type:

* java \-version  
* mvn \-version

If you see version numbers for both, you're ready to code\!

**Basic Commands for running the Test**

* **Running the full suite:**  
  Bash  
  mvn clean test

* **Running with specific tags:**  
  The framework supports tagging (e.g., @smoke, @regression, @auth).  
  Bash  
  mvn clean test \-Dcucumber.filter.tags="@auth"

* **Running a specific feature file:**  
  Bash  
  mvn clean test \-Dcucumber.features="src/test/resources/features/advanced\_interactions.feature"

* **Overriding the browser:**  
  If the framework is configured with a browser parameter in the BaseTest.  
  Bash  
  mvn clean test \-Dbrowser=firefox

## **Industry Standards, Design Patterns, and Best Practices**

For a project to impress a technical interviewer, it must demonstrate an understanding of the "why" behind the code, not just the "how." This framework incorporates several advanced design patterns and best practices.43

### **The Factory and Singleton Patterns**

The DriverFactory utilizes the Factory pattern to instantiate different browser drivers (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) based on a configuration parameter. This decouples the browser choice from the test scripts. Additionally, the DriverManager uses a ThreadLocal Singleton approach to ensure that each thread has its own dedicated WebDriver instance, which is the cornerstone of stable parallel execution.22

### **Strategic Use of Implicit and Explicit Waits**

The framework avoids the "anti-pattern" of Thread.sleep(), which makes tests slow and brittle. Instead, it utilizes a global implicit wait for basic element discovery and surgical explicit waits for complex synchronization events, such as waiting for a loading bar to disappear or an alert to become present.22

### **Data-Driven Testing (DDT)**

By leveraging Gherkin's Scenario Outline and TestNG's @DataProvider, the framework separates test data from the test logic. This allows for high coverage with minimal code, as the same test scenario can be executed against multiple sets of data points.9

### **Error Handling and Resilience**

The framework includes "flaky test" mitigations such as automatic retry logic for transient failures and robust cleanup in the @After hooks. By ensuring the browser is always quit (driver.quit()) after a scenario, the framework prevents memory leaks and stale sessions from impacting subsequent tests.15

## **Conclusion: A Benchmark for Test Engineering Excellence**

The project "The-Internet-Automation" represents a peak-level integration of modern Java features, BDD principles, and TestNG's execution power. By successfully automating the forty-four scenarios on the HerokuApp platform, the framework demonstrates a deep mastery over the complexities of web automation—from handling dynamic AJAX content and Shadow DOM to orchestrating parallel execution in a CI/CD environment.

The use of Java 25 LTS ensures that the framework is built on a high-performance, future-proof runtime, while the dual-reporting strategy with ExtentReports and Cucumber-reporting provides unparalleled observability. This framework is not merely a collection of scripts; it is a scalable, resilient, and professional automation architecture designed to meet the demands of enterprise-level software quality assurance.2 For any technical evaluator, this project serves as a clear indicator of a candidate's ability to design and implement sophisticated automation solutions that are readable by stakeholders and technically rigorous for engineers.
